The Bobo croaker (Pseudotolithus elongatus) attains a maximum recorded body length of 62.5 centimeters [Li = 62.5 centimeters], a value that places it among the larger sciaenids inhabiting coastal West African waters. Field surveys indicate that individuals can achieve this ultimate total length after several years of steady somatic growth, though most adults encountered in commercial catches are considerably smaller. The species exhibits rapid early development, with newly hatched larvae emerging from pelagic eggs that measure approximately 0.59 millimeters in diameter. The wet weight of a neonate immediately after eclosion is calculated at 0.000108 grams [Wwb = 0.000108 grams], reflecting the modest yolk reserves available at the start of the lecithotrophic phase. These buoyant eggs and yolk-sac larvae drift within the planktonic community, where temperature plays a critical role in governing developmental rates and subsequent survival.

Sexual maturation in Bobo croaker is first detected when individuals reach a total length of 19.1 centimeters [Lp = 19.1 centimeters], a size typically achieved during the second year of life under prevailing thermal conditions. At this length at puberty, the corresponding wet weight of the fish is approximately 57 grams [Wwp = approximately 57 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions specific to this species. The onset of gonadal recrudescence marks a clear physiological transition from the immature juvenile phase to the reproductively viable adult stage, though first spawning does not occur immediately upon reaching this size threshold. Growth continues steadily after maturation, and individuals may add considerable mass before attaining their maximum dimensions. The transition from the actively growing, exogenously feeding larva through juvenile recruitment into the adult population involves a series of habitat shifts and dietary changes that accompany the increase in body size.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. At a total length of 29.5 centimeters, females produce approximately 2,000,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2,000,000 eggs per spawning event] and are capable of completing a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year], yielding a substantial annual reproductive investment. This high fecundity, characteristic of many iteroparous sciaenids, compensates for the considerable mortality experienced during the pelagic larval phase. The spawning events are synchronized with seasonal oceanographic cycles, ensuring that the resulting eggs and yolk-dependent larvae encounter favorable temperatures and adequate prey availability during the critical first-feeding period. Field observations confirm that gravid individuals aggregate in nearshore estuarine zones prior to gamete release.

The maximum adult body mass attained by Bobo croaker is approximately 2,200 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,200 grams], representing the ultimate wet weight achieved when the fish has completed its asymptotic growth trajectory. Individuals reaching this size are typically between eight and ten years old, reflecting a growth pattern that slows considerably after sexual maturation. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a typical allometric curve, with the exponent indicating a robust, deep-bodied morphology well suited to demersal foraging. Comparisons with other members of the Sciaenidae family suggest that this ultimate mass is moderate relative to the giant croaker species but substantially larger than many congeners inhabiting similar estuarine environments. The accumulation of lipid reserves in the viscera and musculature supports both reproductive effort and overwintering survival in cooler months.

Longevity records for Pseudotolithus elongatus indicate a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] when maintained under stable thermal conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan is typical for medium-sized sciaenids and reflects a life-history strategy that balances moderate somatic growth with repeated spawning events across several reproductive seasons. The oldest individuals documented in mark-recapture studies correspond to those that have achieved the ultimate total length and wet weight, suggesting that senescence may occur relatively soon after asymptotic size is reached. Natural mortality in the wild is influenced by predation pressure on the pelagic larvae and juvenile fish, as well as by fishing exploitation rates in the coastal demersal fishery. The post-reproductive phase, if it exists, appears to be brief, with most adults succumbing to age-related physiological deterioration shortly after their final spawning season.
